arguments.markdown:
Tesla is a car company with a flat core — revenue fell 2.9% to $94.8bn in FY2025 and was flat at $28.05bn in Q3 2026 — while its two growth stories, energy storage and autonomy, are respectively shrinking and not yet monetised [S3][S4].

**What it sells, to whom, how the money flows.** Tesla builds BEVs (Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck; Model S and X were discontinued in mid-2026), sells direct to consumers, and adds Megapack and Powerwall storage plus services: used cars, collision repair, paid Supercharging and insurance [S3][S4]. It reports two segments, automotive (absorbing services and regulatory credits) and energy [S3]. FY2025 automotive sales fell 9% on 8% fewer cash deliveries and a lower average selling price, offset by services +19% and energy +27% [S3]. In 2026 the driver changed: 9M revenue $78.7bn, +12.5%, with automotive sales +13% against a changeover-depressed base, services +41% and energy −6%; Q3 revenue $28.05bn, flat year on year [S4].

Revenue mix, $m, from the FY2025 10-K [S3] for 2023-2025 and the Q3 2026 10-Q [S4] for 9M 2026:

| Revenue line ($m) | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | 9M 2026 | Share FY2023 → 9M 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive sales, ex-credits | 80,629 | 74,307 | 67,533 | 55,573 | 83% → 71% | [S3][S4] |
| Regulatory credits | 1,790 | 2,763 | 1,993 | 639 | 2% → 1% | [S3][S4] |
| Energy generation and storage | 6,035 | 10,086 | 12,771 | 8,428 | 6% → 11% | [S3][S4] |
| Services and other | 8,319 | 10,534 | 12,530 | 12,931 | 9% → 16% | [S3][S4] |
| Total revenue | 96,773 | 97,690 | 94,827 | 78,669 | 100% | [S3][S4] |

Shares are calculated from the filed figures; automotive sales are net of credits, which the filing reports separately.

**What is actually growing.** Services is now the fastest-growing line, +41% in 9M 2026 to $12.9bn and 16.4% of revenue, on used-vehicle volume and pricing, collision and paid Supercharging [S4]. Energy, the 2023-25 star (6% of revenue in 2023, 13.5% in 2025), shrank 6% in 9M 2026 and 16% in Q3 as Megapack average selling prices fell, Powerwall deployments dropped and $339m of tariff refunds were passed to customers [S3][S4]. Regulatory credits, 2.8% of 2024 revenue, fell 73% in Q3 2026 to $113m and Tesla reversed $475m of previously recognised credit revenue for contractual returns [S4]: the July 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act repealed consumer EV credits and restricted the credit programmes Tesla sells into [S3]. The mix matters because automotive gross margin fell from 19.4% in 2023 to 17.8% in 2025 before recovering to 18.7% in 9M 2026 [S3][S4]: the car business is no longer compounding, so the equity now rests on autonomy and Optimus rather than the current P&L.

**Product and demand.** Demand is concentrated and old. The Model Y and Model 3 were 69% and 28% of Q3 2026 deliveries, leaving 3% for Cybertruck and everything else, and Cox calls both "long-running products" [S22]. US demand fell sharply once credits expired: Q3 2026 US EV sales were 262,649, down 39.5% year on year but up 6.1% on Q2 [S22]. Tesla's US volume fell 20% against that 39.5% decline, so it gained share inside a smaller market, reaching 54% from 50.5% in Q2 [S22][S24]. Europe is the reverse: January 2026 registrations fell 17% to 8,075, the thirteenth consecutive monthly decline, while the EU BEV market grew 14% [S30]. No order backlog or regional revenue split is disclosed [S3].

**Robotaxi and FSD: deployed, but small.** Tesla has run a public driverless service since June 2025 and operates in six US metros — Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando and Tampa — against Waymo's fifteen; San Francisco Bay Area rides still require a safety driver [S25]. Nevada granted a permit for up to 5,000 vehicles in Las Vegas on 20 August 2026 with no service start as of 26 October, and Tesla says Cybercab service opens in Dallas in November 2026 [S25]. Company claims of unsupervised scale are partially verified: third-party trackers confirm the city list and the California safety-driver requirement, not fleet size or utilisation. The only disclosed financial proxy is $4.08bn of deferred revenue tied to FSD, connectivity and Supercharging at 30 September 2026, up 5% in nine months on a $78.7bn revenue base [S4] — unverified as FSD economics, since FSD revenue is folded into automotive sales.

**Policy and litigation.** NHTSA escalated its FSD reduced-visibility probe to Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026, covering 3.2 million 2016-2026 vehicles and one step short of a recall [S21][S23]. Tesla says it is cooperating with government investigations, including DOJ and SEC matters, and that no agency has concluded wrongdoing [S3]. Remedy cost is not disclosed.

**Governance.** Shareholders approved the 2025 CEO Performance Award on 6 November 2025 with 75% support among voting shares; it is worth close to $1 trillion if market-capitalisation and product milestones are met [S26]. The 10-K concedes the award's product goals are designed to focus Musk's time and that misalignment could waste capital [S3]. His shareholding and board independence are not disclosed in the sections reviewed — a gap.

**Milestones.** 4 Jul 2025: OBBBA repeals US consumer EV credits [S3]. 6 Nov 2025: shareholders approve the CEO award [S26]. 18 Mar 2026: NHTSA opens EA26002 [S23]. Mid-2026: Model S and Model X discontinued [S4]. 20 Aug 2026: Nevada permits up to 5,000 Las Vegas robotaxis [S25]. Sep 2026: Cybercab rollout begins [S4]. 22 Oct 2026: Q3 credits −73%, $475m reversal [S4]. 30 Oct 2026: response due to NHTSA's Cybercab certification audit [S25].

Confidence: medium. Segment figures come from audited filings, but robotaxi scale and city-level operations rest on third-party trackers, and Tesla does not disclose FSD revenue, robotaxi revenue or regional volumes.

arguments.markdown:
Tesla is a car company with a flat core — revenue fell 2.9% to $94.8bn in FY2025 and was flat at $28.05bn in Q3 2026 — while energy storage shrinks and autonomy is not yet monetised [S3][S4].

**What it sells, to whom, how the money flows.** Tesla builds BEVs (Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck; Model S and X were discontinued in mid-2026) and sells direct to consumers, plus Megapack and Powerwall storage and services — used cars, collision repair, paid Supercharging, insurance [S3][S4]. It reports two segments: automotive, which absorbs services and regulatory credits, and energy [S3]. FY2025 automotive sales fell 9% on 8% fewer cash deliveries and lower average selling prices, offset by services +19% and energy +27% [S3]. In 2026 the driver changed: 9M revenue $78.7bn (+12.5%), automotive sales +13% against a changeover-depressed base, services +41%, energy −6%; Q3 revenue $28.05bn, flat [S4].

Revenue mix, $m:

| Revenue line ($m) | FY2023 [S3] | FY2024 [S3] | FY2025 [S3] | 9M 2026 [S4] | Share FY2023 → 9M 2026 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive sales, ex-credits | 80,629 | 74,307 | 67,533 | 55,573 | 83% → 71% | [S3][S4] |
| Regulatory credits | 1,790 | 2,763 | 1,993 | 639 | 2% → 1% | [S3][S4] |
| Energy generation and storage | 6,035 | 10,086 | 12,771 | 8,428 | 6% → 11% | [S3][S4] |
| Services and other | 8,319 | 10,534 | 12,530 | 12,931 | 9% → 16% | [S3][S4] |
| Total revenue | 96,773 | 97,690 | 94,827 | 78,669 | 100% | [S3][S4] |

Shares are calculated from the filed figures; automotive sales are net of credits, which the filing reports separately.

**What is actually growing.** Services is the fastest-growing line, +41% to $12.9bn in 9M 2026 and 16.4% of revenue, on used-vehicle volume and pricing, collision and Supercharging [S4]. Energy, 6% of revenue in 2023 and 13.5% in 2025, shrank 6% in 9M 2026 and 16% in Q3 as Megapack prices fell, Powerwall deployments dropped and $339m of tariff refunds were passed to customers [S3][S4]. Regulatory credits fell 73% in Q3 2026 to $113m and Tesla reversed $475m of previously recognised credit revenue for contractual returns [S4]; the July 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act repealed consumer EV credits and restricted the credit programmes Tesla sells into [S3]. Automotive gross margin fell from 19.4% in 2023 to 17.8% in 2025, recovering to 18.7% in 9M 2026 [S3][S4] — the car business is no longer compounding, so for an investor the equity now rests on autonomy and Optimus rather than the current P&L.

**Product and demand.** Demand is concentrated and old: the Model Y and Model 3 were 69% and 28% of Q3 2026 deliveries, leaving 3% for Cybertruck and everything else [S22]. US EV sales fell 39.5% year on year to 262,649 in Q3 2026 after credits expired, though they rose 6.1% on Q2 [S22]; Tesla's US volume fell 20% against that 39.5% decline, so it gained share inside a smaller market, reaching 54% from 50.5% in Q2 [S22][S24]. Europe is the reverse: January 2026 registrations fell 17% to 8,075, the thirteenth consecutive monthly decline, while the EU BEV market grew 14% [S30]. No order backlog or regional revenue split is disclosed [S3].

**Robotaxi and FSD: deployed, but small.** Tesla has run a public driverless service since June 2025 and operates in six US metros — Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa — against Waymo's fifteen; San Francisco Bay Area rides still require a safety driver [S25]. Nevada permitted up to 5,000 vehicles in Las Vegas on 20 August 2026, with no service start as of 26 October, and Tesla says Cybercab service opens in Dallas in November 2026 [S25]. Claims of unsupervised scale are partially verified: trackers confirm the city list and the California safety-driver rule, not fleet size or utilisation. The only disclosed financial proxy is $4.08bn of deferred revenue tied to FSD, connectivity and Supercharging at 30 September 2026, up 5% in nine months on a $78.7bn revenue base [S4] — unverified as FSD economics because FSD revenue sits inside automotive sales.

**Policy and litigation.** NHTSA escalated its FSD reduced-visibility probe to Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026, covering 3.2 million 2016-2026 vehicles and one step short of a recall [S21][S23]. Tesla says it is cooperating with DOJ and SEC investigations and that no agency has concluded wrongdoing [S3]. Remedy cost is not disclosed.

**Governance.** Shareholders approved the 2025 CEO Performance Award on 6 November 2025 with 75% support among voting shares, worth close to $1 trillion if market-capitalisation and product milestones are met [S26]; the 10-K concedes the product goals are designed to focus Musk's time and that misalignment could waste capital [S3]. His shareholding and board independence are not disclosed in the sections reviewed — a gap.

**Milestones.** 4 Jul 2025: OBBBA repeals US consumer EV credits [S3]. 6 Nov 2025: CEO award approved [S26]. 18 Mar 2026: NHTSA opens EA26002 [S23]. 20 Aug 2026: Nevada permits 5,000 Las Vegas robotaxis [S25]. Sep 2026: Cybercab rollout begins; Model S and X axed mid-year [S4]. 30 Oct 2026: NHTSA Cybercab certification response due [S25].

Confidence: medium — segment data are audited filings, but robotaxi scale rests on third-party trackers and Tesla discloses neither FSD nor robotaxi revenue.

Grid storage is the genuinely fast market: BNEF expects 158 GW / 459 GWh of deployments in 2026, up 41% on the 112 GW installed in 2025 [S28].

BYD's September 2026 sales were 463,561, +17%, with exports up 153.9% to 179,877 and 9M volume of 3.13m still 4% below 2025 [S29]. Xiaomi is the credible new entrant but has stalled: 31,267 units in July 2026 and 216,322 in January-July, only 39% of a 550,000 target [S27].

BYD's exports are growing 154% and its Hungarian plant was due to start production in November-December 2026, which would sidestep the EU's ~27% duty on Chinese BEVs, the protection Tesla currently enjoys in Europe [S29]. In autonomy the threat is Waymo: 15 metros to Tesla's six, public driverless service in Las Vegas from September 2026 and a $5bn debt raise in October [S25].

arguments.markdown:
**Tesla stabilised revenue in Q3 2026 but not earnings: the top line was flat at $28,046M, operating income fell 56% to $718M, and free cash flow stayed positive only because capex is running well behind Tesla's own plan [S4][S38].**

**The quarter.** Revenue of $28,046M was flat year over year (−0.2%) [S4]. Automotive sales fell 1% to $20,094M while regulatory credits collapsed 73% to $113M from $417M [S4]. Services and other grew 33% to $4,605M; energy fell 16% to $2,881M [S4]. Total gross margin rose to 19.6% from 18.0% [S4], and automotive gross margin excluding credits — automotive sales of $20,094M less cost of automotive sales of $16,570M — was 17.5% against 14.7% a year earlier [S4]; strip out the $260M of IEEPA tariff refunds booked to automotive cost of revenue and the underlying figure is 16.2% [S4]. Operating income fell 56% because operating expenses rose 39% to $4,776M and R&D rose 69% to $2,761M [S4][S38]. Net income was $787M (−43%), diluted EPS $0.22, non-GAAP EPS $0.48 against a $0.45 consensus [S4][S40][S38].

**Earnings quality.** Three items flatter the quarter. Tariff refunds added $526M to energy and $260M to automotive cost of revenue but cut energy revenue by $339M — a net gross-profit benefit of $447M, 8% of the $5,494M reported [S4]. Tesla reversed $475M of previously recognised regulatory-credit revenue for contractual returns of delivered credits [S4]. And GAAP net income includes a $288M bitcoin gain less a $142M SpaceX equity loss, $146M or 15% of the $956M pretax profit [S38][S4]. Stock-based compensation was $1.17B in the quarter and $4.30B over twelve months, against TTM net income of $3.22B [S38][S4]. Shares outstanding rose to 3,953M at 30 September from 3,751M at 31 December 2025, up 5.4% in nine months without an equity offering; 713M of those shares sit outside the 3,240M basic EPS denominator as unearned awards [S4].

**Volume.** Deliveries were 486,532 in Q3 2026, down 2.1% year over year and below the 497,099 record [S38][S36]; Q2 2026 was over 480,000 and Q1 over 358,000 [S34][S37]; Q4 2025 was 418,227 and FY2025 1,636,129, down 8.6% [S36]. The pattern is shrinking annually in 2025, recovering through the first half of 2026, negative again in Q3, with "other models" down 48% after the Model S/X sunset [S38]. Energy storage deployments were 8.8, 13.5 and 13.7 GWh across the three quarters — 36.0 GWh in nine months against 32.5 GWh, up 11% [S37][S34][S35][S36]. Q3 deployment volume rose 10% while energy revenue fell 16%: pricing and mix, not volume, drove that decline [S4][S38].

**Cash and capex.** Nine-month operating cash flow was $14,897M against $10,934M, capex $13,014M against $6,134M, leaving free cash flow of $1,883M against $4,800M [S4]. On a trailing basis operating cash flow of $18,710M covers capex of $15,407M 1.21x, for free cash flow of $3,303M [S4]. The third quarter alone produced capex of $4.73B and free cash flow of $1.53B against $3.99B a year earlier [S38]. Cash and investments were $45.45B against debt of $9.27B, or net cash of $36.18B [S4]. Tesla guides 2026 capex above $20B [S4]; $13.01B through nine months leaves $6.99B for the fourth quarter, and the shareholder letter reportedly guides above $25B, which would require $11.99B in a single quarter [S38]. Free cash flow covers capex today, but not by enough to absorb a step-up of that size.

**Funding without dilution.** Liquidity of $45.45B, net cash of $36.18B and $30B of credit agreements signed in September 2026 [S4] cover more than two years of $20B capex without issuing equity, and Tesla pays no dividend and buys back no stock [S1][S2][S3]. The 10-Q nonetheless warns that heightened capex "will necessitate additional funding beyond our operating cash flow" [S4]; drawing the full $30B at the 5.04% ten-year yield [S14] would cost $1.51B a year, 44% of TTM operating income. Disclosed commitments are small: $2.0B into SpaceX equity in March 2026 and $1.95B of stock and awards for an AI hardware acquisition in Q2 2026 [S4]. Dilution risk here is compensation, not capital raising.

**The variable that moves the outcome most** is automotive gross profit, not volume: each 100bp of automotive gross margin on $80.4B of annualised automotive sales is $804M, 23% of TTM operating income of $3,466M [S4]. Credits can no longer cushion it — remaining performance obligations fell from $841M at December 2025 to $384M at September 2026 [S3][S4] — so auto margin must stand on cost, mix and FSD subscription revenue alone.

**For the investor:** the reported business now earns $0.91 a share and generates free cash flow equal to 0.2% of its market value [S4][S5]. Any earnings recovery large enough to matter has to come from energy, FSD or robotaxi, not from cars.

**Tesla has re-rated, not de-rated.** Its P/E ran 72.8x in 2021, 34.0x in 2022, 57.8x in 2023, 204.6x in 2024 and 420.8x in 2025, and is 444x today; EV/Sales ran 7.3x, 5.0x, 8.7x, 14.7x and 16.5x over the same years, and is 15.1x today [S1–S5]. At BYD's 0.89x that automotive business is worth $81B; at Rivian's 2.5x, $228B. Energy at 5–8x is $61–98B, and net cash adds $36.18B. The residual is $1.24–1.42 trillion — 77–89% of the market cap, or $312–359 per share — paid for businesses with no separately reported revenue [S4][S39][S11]. Put the other way, at the mega-cap tech median of 27.7x the current market cap requires $57.7B of net income, 17.9x the $3.22B earned over twelve months [S15–S20][S4].

Base $164: automotive at 4x ($365B), energy at 12x ($147B), net cash, plus $100B for FSD and robotaxi. Bull $473: automotive at 6x ($548B), energy at 15x ($184B), net cash, plus $1.1 trillion for robotaxi and Optimus. Weighted 30/45/25 the band gives $211, 48% below the price — the market is already at 85% of the bull case.

**Counter-evidence.** The Street median target is $430–446, above spot, on 43 analysts with a $128–600 range [S42]. Operationally the option is not empty: Q3 deliveries of 486,532 beat the 461,974 consensus, active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74M (+67%), robotaxi logged about two million unsupervised miles and management cites its largest order backlog in four years [S38]. Consensus FY2026 EPS has been cut from $1.89 to $1.37, which argues the estimate risk is to the downside, not that the multiple is wrong [S41].

**Confidence: medium-low.** The 77–89% optionality share is robust to any reasonable automotive multiple; the level of the band is not, because there is no listed peer for robotaxi and the Street's median sits 6–10% above spot. What would change the call is evidence that robotaxi revenue is scaling: incremental evidence, quarterly, would move the bull case toward the base case — the reverse of what the reported financials show today.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business (business, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 5,299 characters)
Tesla is a car company with a flat core — revenue fell 2.9% to $94.8bn in FY2025 and was flat at $28.05bn in Q3 2026 — while energy storage shrinks and autonomy is not yet monetised [S3][S4].

**What it sells, to whom, how the money flows.** Tesla builds BEVs (Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck; Model S and X were discontinued in mid-2026) and sells direct to consumers, plus Megapack and Powerwall storage and services — used cars, collision repair, paid Supercharging, insurance [S3][S4]. It reports two segments: automotive, which absorbs services and regulatory credits, and energy [S3]. FY2025 automotive sales fell 9% on 8% fewer cash deliveries and lower average selling prices, offset by services +19% and energy +27% [S3]. In 2026 the driver changed: 9M revenue $78.7bn (+12.5%), automotive sales +13% against a changeover-depressed base, services +41%, energy −6%; Q3 revenue $28.05bn, flat [S4].

Revenue mix, $m:

Shares are calculated from the filed figures; automotive sales are net of credits, which the filing reports separately.

**What is actually growing.** Services is the fastest-growing line, +41% to $12.9bn in 9M 2026 and 16.4% of revenue, on used-vehicle volume and pricing, collision and Supercharging [S4]. Energy, 6% of revenue in 2023 and 13.5% in 2025, shrank 6% in 9M 2026 and 16% in Q3 as Megapack prices fell, Powerwall deployments dropped and $339m of tariff refunds were passed to customers [S3][S4]. Regulatory credits fell 73% in Q3 2026 to $113m and Tesla reversed $475m of previously recognised credit revenue for contractual returns [S4]; the July 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act repealed consumer EV credits and restricted the credit programmes Tesla sells into [S3]. Automotive gross margin fell from 19.4% in 2023 to 17.8% in 2025, recovering to 18.7% in 9M 2026 [S3][S4] — the car business is no longer compounding, so for an investor the equity now rests on autonomy and Optimus rather than the current P&L.

**Product and demand.** Demand is concentrated and old: the Model Y and Model 3 were 69% and 28% of Q3 2026 deliveries, leaving 3% for Cybertruck and everything else [S22]. US EV sales fell 39.5% year on year to 262,649 in Q3 2026 after credits expired, though they rose 6.1% on Q2 [S22]; Tesla's US volume fell 20% against that 39.5% decline, so it gained share inside a smaller market, reaching 54% from 50.5% in Q2 [S22][S24]. Europe is the reverse: January 2026 registrations fell 17% to 8,075, the thirteenth consecutive monthly decline, while the EU BEV market grew 14% [S30]. No order backlog or regional revenue split is disclosed [S3].

**Robotaxi and FSD: deployed, but small.** Tesla has run a public driverless service since June 2025 and operates in six US metros — Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa — against Waymo's fifteen; San Francisco Bay Area rides still require a safety driver [S25]. Nevada permitted up to 5,000 vehicles in Las Vegas on 20 August 2026, with no service start as of 26 October, and Tesla says Cybercab service opens in Dallas in November 2026 [S25]. Claims of unsupervised scale are partially verified: trackers confirm the city list and the California safety-driver rule, not fleet size or utilisation. The only disclosed financial proxy is $4.08bn of deferred revenue tied to FSD, connectivity and Supercharging at 30 September 2026, up 5% in nine months on a $78.7bn revenue base [S4] — unverified as FSD economics because FSD revenue sits inside automotive sales.

**Policy and litigation.** NHTSA escalated its FSD reduced-visibility probe to Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026, covering 3.2 million 2016-2026 vehicles and one step short of a recall [S21][S23]. Tesla says it is cooperating with DOJ and SEC investigations and that no agency has concluded wrongdoing [S3]. Remedy cost is not disclosed.

**Governance.** Shareholders approved the 2025 CEO Performance Award on 6 November 2025 with 75% support among voting shares, worth close to $1 trillion if market-capitalisation and product milestones are met [S26]; the 10-K concedes the product goals are designed to focus Musk's time and that misalignment could waste capital [S3]. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financials (financials, revision 2 by Fundamentals Analyst, 6,165 characters)
**Tesla stabilised revenue in Q3 2026 but not earnings: the top line was flat at $28,046M, operating income fell 56% to $718M, and free cash flow stayed positive only because capex is running well behind Tesla's own plan [S4][S38].**

**The quarter.** Revenue of $28,046M was flat year over year (−0.2%) [S4]. Automotive sales fell 1% to $20,094M while regulatory credits collapsed 73% to $113M from $417M [S4]. Services and other grew 33% to $4,605M; energy fell 16% to $2,881M [S4]. Total gross margin rose to 19.6% from 18.0% [S4], and automotive gross margin excluding credits — automotive sales of $20,094M less cost of automotive sales of $16,570M — was 17.5% against 14.7% a year earlier [S4]; strip out the $260M of IEEPA tariff refunds booked to automotive cost of revenue and the underlying figure is 16.2% [S4]. Operating income fell 56% because operating expenses rose 39% to $4,776M and R&D rose 69% to $2,761M [S4][S38]. Net income was $787M (−43%), diluted EPS $0.22, non-GAAP EPS $0.48 against a $0.45 consensus [S4][S40][S38].

**Earnings quality.** Three items flatter the quarter. Tariff refunds added $526M to energy and $260M to automotive cost of revenue but cut energy revenue by $339M — a net gross-profit benefit of $447M, 8% of the $5,494M reported [S4]. Tesla reversed $475M of previously recognised regulatory-credit revenue for contractual returns of delivered credits [S4]. And GAAP net income includes a $288M bitcoin gain less a $142M SpaceX equity loss, $146M or 15% of the $956M pretax profit [S38][S4]. Stock-based compensation was $1.17B in the quarter and $4.30B over twelve months, against TTM net income of $3.22B [S38][S4]. Shares outstanding rose to 3,953M at 30 September from 3,751M at 31 December 2025, up 5.4% in nine months without an equity offering; 713M of those shares sit outside the 3,240M basic EPS denominator as unearned awards [S4].

**Volume.** Deliveries were 486,532 in Q3 2026, down 2.1% year over year and below the 497,099 record [S38][S36]; Q2 2026 was over 480,000 and Q1 over 358,000 [S34][S37]; Q4 2025 was 418,227 and FY2025 1,636,129, down 8.6% [S36]. The pattern is shrinking annually in 2025, recovering through the first half of 2026, negative again in Q3, with "other models" down 48% after the Model S/X sunset [S38]. Energy storage deployments were 8.8, 13.5 and 13.7 GWh across the three quarters — 36.0 GWh in nine months against 32.5 GWh, up 11% [S37][S34][S35][S36]. Q3 deployment volume rose 10% while energy revenue fell 16%: pricing and mix, not volume, drove that decline [S4][S38].

**Cash and capex.** Nine-month operating cash flow was $14,897M against $10,934M, capex $13,014M against $6,134M, leaving free cash flow of $1,883M against $4,800M [S4]. On a trailing basis operating cash flow of $18,710M covers capex of $15,407M 1.21x, for free cash flow of $3,303M [S4]. The third quarter alone produced capex of $4.73B and free cash flow of $1.53B against $3.99B a year earlier [S38]. Cash and investments were $45.45B against debt of $9.27B, or net cash of $36.18B [S4]. Tesla guides 2026 capex above $20B [S4]; $13.01B through nine months leaves $6.99B for the fourth quarter, and the shareholder letter reportedly guides above $25B, which would require $11.99B in a single quarter [S38]. Free cash flow covers capex today, but not by enough to absorb a step-up of that size.

**Funding without dilution.** Liquidity of $45.45B, net cash of $36.18B and $30B of credit agreements signed in September 2026 [S4] cover more than two years of $20B capex without issuing equity, and Tesla pays no dividend and buys back no stock [S1][S2][S3]. The 10-Q nonetheless warns that heightened capex "will necessitate additional funding beyond our operating cash flow" [S4]; drawing the full $30B at the 5.04% ten-year yield [S14] would cost $1.51B a year, 44% of TTM operating income. Disclosed commitments are small: $2.0B into SpaceX equity in March 2026 and $1.95B of stock and awards for an AI hardware acquisition in Q2 2026 [S4]. Dilution risk here is compensation, not capital raising.

**The variable that moves the outcome most** is automotive gross profit, not volume: each 100bp of automotive gross margin on $80.4B of annualised automotive sales is $804M, 23% of TTM operating income of $3,466M [S4]. Credits can no longer cushion it — remaining performance obligations fell from $841M at December 2025 to $384M at September 2026 [S3][S4] — so auto margin must stand on cost, mix and FSD subscription revenue alone.

**For the investor:** the reported business now earns $0.91 a share and generates free cash flow equal to 0.2% of its market value [S4][S5]. Any earnings recovery large enough to matter has to come from energy, FSD or robotaxi, not from cars.

Energy, 6% of revenue in 2023 and 13.5% in 2025, shrank 6% in 9M 2026 and 16% in Q3 as Megapack prices fell, Powerwall deployments dropped and $339m of tariff refunds were passed to customers [S3][S4]. Regulatory credits fell 73% in Q3 2026 to $113m and Tesla reversed $475m of previously recognised credit revenue for contractual returns [S4]; the July 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act repealed consumer EV credits and restricted the credit programmes Tesla sells into [S3]. Automotive gross margin fell from 19.4% in 2023 to 17.8% in 2025, recovering to 18.7% in 9M 2026 [S3][S4] — the car business is no longer compounding, so for an investor the equity now rests on autonomy and Optimus rather than the current P&L.

No order backlog or regional revenue split is disclosed [S3].

## Competition and market (competition, revision 4 by Market Analyst, changed since the previous version, 5,685 characters)

Software is an option, not a moat: $4.08bn of FSD-related deferred revenue against $78.7bn of 9M revenue [S4]. Two nameplates were 97% of Q3 2026 deliveries [S22]. **Counter-evidence: the case that Tesla loses the auto profit pool and has not monetised AI.** Revenue fell 2.9% in 2025 and was flat in Q3 2026 [S3][S4]; US volume fell 20% in a market down 39.5% [S22]; Europe has declined for thirteen consecutive months [S30]; BYD leads on volume at half the price with the same gross margin [S31][S29]. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financials (financials, revision 2 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 6,165 characters)
**Tesla stabilised revenue in Q3 2026 but not earnings: the top line was flat at $28,046M, operating income fell 56% to $718M, and free cash flow stayed positive only because capex is running well behind Tesla's own plan [S4][S38].**

**The quarter.** Revenue of $28,046M was flat year over year (−0.2%) [S4]. Automotive sales fell 1% to $20,094M while regulatory credits collapsed 73% to $113M from $417M [S4]. Services and other grew 33% to $4,605M; energy fell 16% to $2,881M [S4]. Total gross margin rose to 19.6% from 18.0% [S4], and automotive gross margin excluding credits — automotive sales of $20,094M less cost of automotive sales of $16,570M — was 17.5% against 14.7% a year earlier [S4]; strip out the $260M of IEEPA tariff refunds booked to automotive cost of revenue and the underlying figure is 16.2% [S4]. Operating income fell 56% because operating expenses rose 39% to $4,776M and R&D rose 69% to $2,761M [S4][S38]. Net income was $787M (−43%), diluted EPS $0.22, non-GAAP EPS $0.48 against a $0.45 consensus [S4][S40][S38].

**Earnings quality.** Three items flatter the quarter. Tariff refunds added $526M to energy and $260M to automotive cost of revenue but cut energy revenue by $339M — a net gross-profit benefit of $447M, 8% of the $5,494M reported [S4]. Tesla reversed $475M of previously recognised regulatory-credit revenue for contractual returns of delivered credits [S4]. And GAAP net income includes a $288M bitcoin gain less a $142M SpaceX equity loss, $146M or 15% of the $956M pretax profit [S38][S4]. Stock-based compensation was $1.17B in the quarter and $4.30B over twelve months, against TTM net income of $3.22B [S38][S4]. Shares outstanding rose to 3,953M at 30 September from 3,751M at 31 December 2025, up 5.4% in nine months without an equity offering; 713M of those shares sit outside the 3,240M basic EPS denominator as unearned awards [S4].

**Volume.** Deliveries were 486,532 in Q3 2026, down 2.1% year over year and below the 497,099 record [S38][S36]; Q2 2026 was over 480,000 and Q1 over 358,000 [S34][S37]; Q4 2025 was 418,227 and FY2025 1,636,129, down 8.6% [S36]. The pattern is shrinking annually in 2025, recovering through the first half of 2026, negative again in Q3, with "other models" down 48% after the Model S/X sunset [S38]. Energy storage deployments were 8.8, 13.5 and 13.7 GWh across the three quarters — 36.0 GWh in nine months against 32.5 GWh, up 11% [S37][S34][S35][S36]. Q3 deployment volume rose 10% while energy revenue fell 16%: pricing and mix, not volume, drove that decline [S4][S38].

**Cash and capex.** Nine-month operating cash flow was $14,897M against $10,934M, capex $13,014M against $6,134M, leaving free cash flow of $1,883M against $4,800M [S4]. On a trailing basis operating cash flow of $18,710M covers capex of $15,407M 1.21x, for free cash flow of $3,303M [S4]. The third quarter alone produced capex of $4.73B and free cash flow of $1.53B against $3.99B a year earlier [S38]. Cash and investments were $45.45B against debt of $9.27B, or net cash of $36.18B [S4]. Tesla guides 2026 capex above $20B [S4]; $13.01B through nine months leaves $6.99B for the fourth quarter, and the shareholder letter reportedly guides above $25B, which would require $11.99B in a single quarter [S38]. Free cash flow covers capex today, but not by enough to absorb a step-up of that size.

**Funding without dilution.** Liquidity of $45.45B, net cash of $36.18B and $30B of credit agreements signed in September 2026 [S4] cover more than two years of $20B capex without issuing equity, and Tesla pays no dividend and buys back no stock [S1][S2][S3]. The 10-Q nonetheless warns that heightened capex "will necessitate additional funding beyond our operating cash flow" [S4]; drawing the full $30B at the 5.04% ten-year yield [S14] would cost $1.51B a year, 44% of TTM operating income. Disclosed commitments are small: $2.0B into SpaceX equity in March 2026 and $1.95B of stock and awards for an AI hardware acquisition in Q2 2026 [S4]. Dilution risk here is compensation, not capital raising.

**The variable that moves the outcome most** is automotive gross profit, not volume: each 100bp of automotive gross margin on $80.4B of annualised automotive sales is $804M, 23% of TTM operating income of $3,466M [S4]. Credits can no longer cushion it — remaining performance obligations fell from $841M at December 2025 to $384M at September 2026 [S3][S4] — so auto margin must stand on cost, mix and FSD subscription revenue alone.

**For the investor:** the reported business now earns $0.91 a share and generates free cash flow equal to 0.2% of its market value [S4][S5]. Any earnings recovery large enough to matter has to come from energy, FSD or robotaxi, not from cars.

## Risks and counter-evidence (risks, revision 3 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 4,478 characters)
**Tesla's equity is a call option on revenue it does not report, and the option is priced above the strike.** 77–89% of the $1,597.8B market capitalisation — $312–359 a share — pays for robotaxi, Optimus and AI with no separately disclosed revenue [S4][S5][S39]. It has slipped: unsupervised FSD is guided to Q2 2027 [S38], and $4.08B of FSD-related deferred revenue grew 5% in nine months against $78.7B of revenue [S4].

**Risks ranked by probability and impact.**

1. **Valuation and optionality (high probability, fatal).** A 444.2x trailing P/E and 15.1x EV/Sales against BYD's 0.89x leave no earnings support; the price sits 146% above the $164 base case [S4][S39]. Signpost: robotaxi revenue disclosed separately.

2. **BYD cost and price competition (high, high).** BYD sold 557,090 BEVs in Q2 2026 against Tesla's 480,126, at a $20,300 average price versus $41,300 and an 18.85% gross margin against Tesla's 18.7% [S31][S32][S29][S4]. Its exports rose 154% in September 2026 and a Hungarian plant was due onstream in November–December 2026, removing the EU's 27% tariff shield [S29].

3. **US demand reset (occurred, medium-high).** US EV sales fell 39.5% to 262,649 in Q3 2026 [S22]; credits fell to $113M from $417M with $475M reversed, and remaining credit obligations dropped from $841M to $384M [S4][S3]. Signpost: Q4 credit revenue below $100M [S4].

4. **Regulatory and recall (medium, high).** NHTSA's EA26002, opened 18 March 2026, covers about 3.2M vehicles and is one step short of a recall; petition DP26010 opened 9 October 2026 [S21][S23][S25]. Signpost: a remedy decision, or Cybercab certification due 30 October 2026 [S25].

5. **Capex and free cash flow (medium, manageable).** Capex of $13,014M in nine months against guidance above $20B — reportedly above $25B — leaves up to $12B for Q4, against trailing free cash flow of $3,303M [S4][S38]. Net cash of $36.18B and $30B of facilities fund it without equity [S4]. Signpost: negative Q4 free cash flow.

6. **Europe share loss (occurred, medium).** January 2026 registrations fell 17% to 8,075, a thirteenth consecutive decline, while the EU BEV market grew 14% [S30].

7. **Governance and key-person (medium, medium).** A CEO award worth close to $1tn was approved on 6 November 2025 with 75% support [S26]; stock-based compensation of $4.30B over twelve months exceeds net income of $3.22B [S38][S4].

8. **Energy commoditisation (medium, medium).** Energy revenue fell 16% in Q3 2026 while deployments rose 10% [S4][S38]; Megapack prices fell in 2025 even as segment margin reached 30.2% [S3][S4]. Signpost: storage margin below 25% [S4].

**The strongest case against this view** is that the option is not empty: the median target is $430–446 across 43 analysts [S42]; Q3 deliveries of 486,532 beat the 461,974 consensus by 5%, FSD subscriptions reached 1.74M, up 67%, robotaxi logged about two million unsupervised miles, and the order backlog is the largest in four years [S38]. Free cash flow 30% lower takes it to $2,312M and the yield from 0.2% to 0.14%; the rating stays Reduce unless Q4 capex turns free cash flow negative [S4][S38].

**What this means for the investor:** every stress case lands below the current price, so the risk is asymmetric until robotaxi economics are disclosed [S4].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## E1 (Market Analyst): Tesla business mix, robotaxi status, competition and market
Tesla's core auto business is flat to shrinking: FY2025 revenue fell 2.9% to $94.8bn and Q3 2026 revenue was flat at $28.05bn. Growth has rotated from regulatory credits and energy storage (both now falling) to low-margin services. Robotaxi is real but small (six US metros vs Waymo's fifteen) and FSD has no disclosed revenue line; the only proxy is $4.08bn of deferred revenue. BYD now leads global BEV volume at roughly half Tesla's ASP with comparable gross margin, and the US EV market shrank 39.5% after credits expired.
Parts: business, competition
Findings:
- FY2025 revenue fell 2.9% to $94.8bn from $97.7bn; automotive sales fell 9% on 8% fewer cash deliveries and lower average selling prices, offset by services +19% and energy +27% [S3]
- Mix shift: automotive sales fell from 83% of revenue in FY2023 to 71% in 9M 2026, services rose from 9% to 16%, energy from 6% to 11% [S3][S4]
- Regulatory credits fell 73% in Q3 2026 to $113m and Tesla reversed $475m of previously recognised credit revenue for contractual returns; the July 2025 OBBBA repealed US consumer EV credits and restricted credit programmes [S4][S3]
- Energy storage revenue fell 16% in Q3 2026 and 6% in 9M 2026 despite 36.0 GWh of deployments, on lower Megapack ASP, lower Powerwall deployments and $339m of tariff refunds passed to customers [S4]
- US EV sales were 262,649 in Q3 2026, down 39.5% YoY at 6.4% share; Tesla's US volume fell 20%, so its share rose to 54% from 50.5% in Q2 2026 [S22][S24]
- Europe is the weak spot: Tesla's January 2026 registrations fell 17% to 8,075, the thirteenth consecutive monthly decline, while the EU BEV market grew 14% [S30]
- Robotaxi operates in six US metros (Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, Tampa) against Waymo's fifteen; San Francisco Bay Area still requires a safety driver; a Nevada permit for up to 5,000 Las Vegas vehicles was granted 20 Aug 2026 with no service start as of 26 Oct 2026 [S25]
- FSD-related deferred revenue was $4.08bn at 30 Sep 2026, up 5% in nine months against $78.7bn of 9M revenue: the only disclosed proxy for FSD monetisation, and Tesla does not break FSD revenue out [S4]
- NHTSA escalated its FSD reduced-visibility probe to Engineering Analysis EA26002 on 18 March 2026, covering about 3.2m 2016-2026 vehicles and one step short of recall; a separate defect petition DP26010 opened 9 Oct 2026 [S21][S23][S25]
- BYD delivered 557,090 BEVs in Q2 2026 against Tesla's 480,126 (16% gap) and 2.26m against 1.64m in 2025; September exports rose 153.9% and H1 gross margin was 18.85% versus Tesla's 18.7% automotive margin [S31][S29][S4]
- Xiaomi delivered 31,267 EVs in July 2026 and 216,322 in January-July, only 39% of a 550,000 annual target: a real entrant but stalled in 2026 [S27]
- BNEF forecasts 158 GW / 459 GWh of global storage deployments in 2026, up 41% on 112 GW in 2025; Tesla's 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026 is 8-10% of that on a run-rate basis (our arithmetic) [S28][S4]
- Shareholders approved the 2025 CEO Performance Award on 6 Nov 2025 with 75% support, worth close to $1tn if market-cap and product milestones are met [S26]
Risks:
- US EV demand stays structurally lower after the consumer credit expired; Tesla volume fell 20% YoY in a market down 39.5% [S22]
- Regulatory credit revenue is now small and reversible: $475m reversed in Q3 2026 and the OBBBA curtailed the programmes [S4][S3]
- A recall-stage NHTSA engineering analysis on FSD covering about 3.2m vehicles could restrict or delay robotaxi expansion [S21][S23]
- BYD and Xiaomi price competition at roughly half Tesla's ASP erodes auto margin, and BYD's Hungarian plant removes the EU tariff shield from late 2026 [S29][S31]
- Energy storage pricing is softening (Megapack ASP fell in 2025 and revenue fell 16% in Q3 2026), so the second engine may commoditise before it scales [S3][S4]
- Governance and key-person risk: a pay award worth close to $1tn tied to product milestones, with the 10-K itself flagging Musk's time allocation [S26][S3]
Scenario drivers:
- Up: unsupervised FSD approved in more states and robotaxi revenue disclosed at scale; automotive gross margin holds 18%+ as volume recovers; storage margin stays above 30% with Megapack price stabilisation [S4]
- Up: US EV demand recovery as Cox reports the reset phase largely over and high petrol prices support EVs [S22]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive summary (executive_summary, revision 1 by Lead Analyst, 3,068 characters)
Tesla closed at $404.22 on 28 October 2026, a $1,597.8B market capitalisation and a $1,561.6B enterprise value against $36.18B of net cash [S5][S4]. The stock sits in a $297.38–498.83 fifty-two-week range, up 13.1% in a month and 35.5% in three, but down 11.0% year to date and 12.4% over twelve months while the S&P 500 rose 12.4% [S5][S12]. With the VIX at 16.91 and the 10-year Treasury at 5.04%, the move is company-specific rather than macro [S13][S14]. Q3 2026 revenue was flat at $28,046M and operating income fell 56% to $718M [S4].

**Verdict: Reduce, zero new capital, 12-month horizon.** Tesla is a flat car business at 15.1x EV/Sales against BYD's 0.89x, with 77–89% of the price — $312–359 a share — resting on robotaxi and AI revenue it does not report [S4][S39]. The weighted band is $62 bear / $164 base / $473 bull, or $211, 48% below spot [S4][S5].

**Three positives.** Net cash of $36.18B, with trailing operating cash flow of $18,710M covering capex of $15,407M 1.21x [S4]. Q3 gross margin rose to 19.6% from 18.0% and automotive margin ex-credits to 17.5% from 14.7% [S4]. US EV share rose to 54% from 50.5% and storage gross margin reached 30.2% [S22][S24][S3][S4].

**Three risks.** The optionality carrying 77–89% of the price has no revenue line, and unsupervised FSD has slipped to Q2 2027 [S4][S38]. BYD sold 557,090 BEVs in Q2 2026 against Tesla's 480,126 at half the average price with an 18.85% gross margin [S31][S29][S32]. NHTSA's EA26002 covers 3.2M vehicles while capex is guided above $20B after $13,014M in nine months [S21][S4].

**Versus consensus.** The Street median target is $430–446 across 43 analysts [S42], but FY2026 consensus EPS has been cut from $1.89 to $1.37 [S41]; we agree with the cuts and disagree with the target, because no listed robotaxi peer exists to anchor the premium.

**Follow-up diligence:** what Tesla's robotaxi operation earned in Q3 2026, and whether the Q4 letter or 10-K will disclose it separately [S4]. **Confidence: medium-low** — the automotive multiple work is robust, the optionality value is not [S39][S42].

**The probability-weighted outcome is $211 a share, 48% below the $404.22 price, because the base case is a flat car business priced for a robotaxi business that has not reported a dollar of revenue [S5][S4][S39].**

**Bull — 25%.** NHTSA closes EA26002 without a recall, Cybercab certification arrives, robotaxi expands beyond its six metros, and FSD converts part of $4.08B of deferred revenue into recognised sales [S25][S4]. Automotive gross margin holds above 18% and storage margin above 30% [S4][S3], so the market pays for the optionality in full. Outcome: $473 a share, +17% [S4]. Signposts: a closed NHTSA docket, a city count above six [S25], and deferred revenue growth above the 5% logged in nine months [S4].

**Base — 45%.** Revenue stays flat, automotive margin ex-credits holds 16–18%, credits stay near the $113M quarterly run rate, capex lands at $20–25B and free cash flow hovers near zero [S4][S38]. **Bear — 30%.** An NHTSA remedy or a robotaxi rollout slipping past 2027 removes the programme from the valuation window [S21][S25]; US volume keeps falling, BYD's Hungarian plant takes European share and storage pricing slides [S29][S4]. Outcome: $62, −85% [S4]. Signposts: a recall notice, a fourteenth monthly European decline [S30], and credit obligations running off from $384M [S4].

**The assumptions that matter, ranked by effect.**

1. Robotaxi and FSD become reported revenue. This is worth $312–359 of today's $404.22, or 77–89% of the market cap [S4][S39]; if it fails, the equity is a $62–164 stock [S4].
2. Automotive gross margin ex-credits holds at 17.5% or better [S4]. Each 100bp on $80.4B of annualised automotive sales is $804M, 23% of trailing operating income of $3,466M [S4].
3. Capex lands near $20B rather than the reported $25B-plus [S4][S38]. Nine-month capex was $13,014M, so the fourth quarter decides whether trailing free cash flow of $3,303M survives [S4].
4. Storage margin holds near 30.2% while energy revenue falls 16% [S3][S4].
5. The US EV market keeps recovering from 262,649 units in Q3 2026, up 6.1% on Q2 [S22].

**Position sizing: zero new capital.** At $404.22 the stock offers 17% upside in the bull case against 59% downside in the base case [S5][S4]. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Risks and counter-evidence (risks, revision 3 by Lead Analyst, 4,478 characters)
**Tesla's equity is a call option on revenue it does not report, and the option is priced above the strike.** 77–89% of the $1,597.8B market capitalisation — $312–359 a share — pays for robotaxi, Optimus and AI with no separately disclosed revenue [S4][S5][S39]. It has slipped: unsupervised FSD is guided to Q2 2027 [S38], and $4.08B of FSD-related deferred revenue grew 5% in nine months against $78.7B of revenue [S4].

**Risks ranked by probability and impact.**

1. **Valuation and optionality (high probability, fatal).** A 444.2x trailing P/E and 15.1x EV/Sales against BYD's 0.89x leave no earnings support; the price sits 146% above the $164 base case [S4][S39]. Signpost: robotaxi revenue disclosed separately.

2. **BYD cost and price competition (high, high).** BYD sold 557,090 BEVs in Q2 2026 against Tesla's 480,126, at a $20,300 average price versus $41,300 and an 18.85% gross margin against Tesla's 18.7% [S31][S32][S29][S4]. Its exports rose 154% in September 2026 and a Hungarian plant was due onstream in November–December 2026, removing the EU's 27% tariff shield [S29].

3. **US demand reset (occurred, medium-high).** US EV sales fell 39.5% to 262,649 in Q3 2026 [S22]; credits fell to $113M from $417M with $475M reversed, and remaining credit obligations dropped from $841M to $384M [S4][S3]. Signpost: Q4 credit revenue below $100M [S4].

4. **Regulatory and recall (medium, high).** NHTSA's EA26002, opened 18 March 2026, covers about 3.2M vehicles and is one step short of a recall; petition DP26010 opened 9 October 2026 [S21][S23][S25]. Signpost: a remedy decision, or Cybercab certification due 30 October 2026 [S25].

5. **Capex and free cash flow (medium, manageable).** Capex of $13,014M in nine months against guidance above $20B — reportedly above $25B — leaves up to $12B for Q4, against trailing free cash flow of $3,303M [S4][S38]. Net cash of $36.18B and $30B of facilities fund it without equity [S4]. Signpost: negative Q4 free cash flow.

6. **Europe share loss (occurred, medium).** January 2026 registrations fell 17% to 8,075, a thirteenth consecutive decline, while the EU BEV market grew 14% [S30].

7. **Governance and key-person (medium, medium).** A CEO award worth close to $1tn was approved on 6 November 2025 with 75% support [S26]; stock-based compensation of $4.30B over twelve months exceeds net income of $3.22B [S38][S4].

8. **Energy commoditisation (medium, medium).** Energy revenue fell 16% in Q3 2026 while deployments rose 10% [S4][S38]; Megapack prices fell in 2025 even as segment margin reached 30.2% [S3][S4]. Signpost: storage margin below 25% [S4].

**The strongest case against this view** is that the option is not empty: the median target is $430–446 across 43 analysts [S42]; Q3 deliveries of 486,532 beat the 461,974 consensus by 5%, FSD subscriptions reached 1.74M, up 67%, robotaxi logged about two million unsupervised miles, and the order backlog is the largest in four years [S38]. Any certification headline can squeeze a bearish position.

**Stress tests.** Revenue 30% lower at today's 15.1x EV/Sales gives $286 a share, −29%, moving the rating from Reduce toward Sell [S4][S5]. A 20% multiple compression to 12.1x gives $325, −20%, leaving the rating unchanged [S4][S5]. Free cash flow 30% lower takes it to $2,312M and the yield from 0.2% to 0.14%; the rating stays Reduce unless Q4 capex turns free cash flow negative [S4][S38].

**What this means for the investor:** every stress case lands below the current price, so the risk is asymmetric until robotaxi economics are disclosed [S4].

Confidence: medium — audited financials and current multiples, but no verifiable robotaxi economics [S4][S25].

**The probability-weighted outcome is $211 a share, 48% below the $404.22 price, because the base case is a flat car business priced for a robotaxi business that has not reported a dollar of revenue [S5][S4][S39].** That weighting supports selling rather than holding: the base case alone is 59% below spot.

**Bull — 25%.** NHTSA closes EA26002 without a recall, Cybercab certification arrives, robotaxi expands beyond its six metros, and FSD converts part of $4.08B of deferred revenue into recognised sales [S25][S4]. Automotive gross margin holds above 18% and storage margin above 30% [S4][S3], so the market pays for the optionality in full. Outcome: $473 a share, +17% [S4]. Signposts: a closed NHTSA docket, a city count above six [S25], and deferred revenue growth above the 5% logged in nine months [S4].

**Base — 45%.** Revenue stays flat, automotive margin ex-credits holds 16–18%, credits stay near the $113M quarterly run rate, capex lands at $20–25B and free cash flow hovers near zero [S4][S38]. Robotaxi stays small and undisclosed. Outcome: $164, −59% [S4]. Signposts: Q4 free cash flow and FY2027 consensus EPS of $1.17 [S40].

**Bear — 30%.** An NHTSA remedy or a robotaxi rollout slipping past 2027 removes the programme from the valuation window [S21][S25]; US volume keeps falling, BYD's Hungarian plant takes European share and storage pricing slides [S29][S4]. Outcome: $62, −85% [S4]. Signposts: a recall notice, a fourteenth monthly European decline [S30], and credit obligations running off from $384M [S4].

**The assumptions that matter, ranked by effect.**

1. Robotaxi and FSD become reported revenue. This is worth $312–359 of today's $404.22, or 77–89% of the market cap [S4][S39]; if it fails, the equity is a $62–164 stock [S4].
2. Automotive gross margin ex-credits holds at 17.5% or better [S4]. Each 100bp on $80.4B of annualised automotive sales is $804M, 23% of trailing operating income of $3,466M [S4].
3. Capex lands near $20B rather than the reported $25B-plus [S4][S38]. Nine-month capex was $13,014M, so the fourth quarter decides whether trailing free cash flow of $3,303M survives [S4].
4. Storage margin holds near 30.2% while energy revenue falls 16% [S3][S4].
5. The US EV market keeps recovering from 262,649 units in Q3 2026, up 6.1% on Q2 [S22].

**Position sizing: zero — Sell.** At $404.22 the stock offers 17% upside in the bull case against 59% base-case and 85% bear-case downside, a probability-weighted −48% [S5][S4]. Existing holders should exit rather than trim, because the base case alone sits far below the current price and no robotaxi revenue is disclosed to anchor a recovery. Revisit only if robotaxi revenue is disclosed at scale, or at the $164 base band [S4].

**Tesla's equity is a call option on revenue it does not report, and the option is priced above the strike.** 77–89% of the $1,597.8B market capitalisation — $312–359 a share — pays for robotaxi, Optimus and AI with no separately disclosed revenue [S4][S5][S39]. **Risks ranked by probability and impact.**

1. **Valuation and optionality (high probability, fatal).** 15.1x EV/Sales against BYD's 0.89x leaves no earnings support; the price sits 146% above the $164 base case [S4][S39]. Signpost: robotaxi revenue disclosed separately.

2. **BYD cost and price competition (high, high).** BYD sold 557,090 BEVs in Q2 2026 against Tesla's 480,126, at a $20,300 average price versus $41,300 and an 18.85% company-wide gross margin against Tesla's 18.7% [S31][S32][S29][S4]. Its exports rose 154% in September 2026 and a Hungarian plant was due onstream in November–December 2026, removing the EU's 27% tariff shield [S29].

3. **US demand reset (occurred, medium-high).** US EV sales fell 39.5% to 262,649 in Q3 2026 [S22]; credits fell to $113M from $417M with $475M reversed, and remaining credit obligations dropped from $841M to $384M [S4][S3]. Signpost: Q4 credit revenue below $100M [S4].

4. **Regulatory and recall (medium, high).** NHTSA's EA26002, opened 18 March 2026, covers about 3.2M vehicles and is one step short of a recall; petition DP26010 opened 9 October 2026 [S21][S23][S25]. Signpost: a remedy decision, or Cybercab certification due 30 October 2026 [S25].

5. **Capex and free cash flow (medium, manageable).** Capex of $13,014M in nine months against guidance above $20B — reportedly above $25B — leaves up to $12B for Q4, against trailing free cash flow of $3,303M [S4][S38]. Net cash of $36.18B and $30B of facilities fund it without equity [S4]. Signpost: negative Q4 free cash flow.

6. **Europe share loss (occurred, medium).** January 2026 registrations fell 17% to 8,075, a thirteenth consecutive decline, while the EU BEV market grew 14% [S30].

7. **Governance and key-person (medium, medium).** A CEO award worth close to $1tn was approved on 6 November 2025 with 75% support [S26]; stock-based compensation of $4.30B over twelve months exceeds net income of $3.22B [S38][S4].

8. **Energy commoditisation (medium, medium).** Energy revenue fell 16% in Q3 2026 while deployments rose 10% [S4][S38]; Megapack prices fell in 2025 even as segment margin reached 30.2% [S3][S4]. Signpost: storage margin below 25% [S4].

A 20% multiple compression to 12.1x gives $325, −20%, which leaves the call Sell [S4][S5]. Free cash flow 30% lower takes it to $2,312M and the yield from 0.2% to 0.14%; a negative Q4 free cash flow would harden the call [S4][S38]. Every stress case lands below the current price, so the risk stays asymmetric until robotaxi economics are disclosed [S4].

{"url":"https://cnevpost.com/2026/02/27/baidu-apollo-go-robotaxi-300000-weekly-rides-expands-to-south-korea/","title":"Baidu's Apollo Go robotaxi hits 300,000 weekly rides as service expands to South Korea","text":"Lei Kang

 •

 Feb 27, 2026, 10:35 AM GMT+8

By February 2026, Apollo Go has delivered over 20 million rides worldwide cumulatively.

(Image credit: Apollo Go)
Baidu announced Thursday that its autonomous ride-hailing platform Apollo Go achieved a weekly order peak exceeding 300,000 trips in the fourth quarter of 2025.
It also announced its official entry into the South Korean market, marking the service's first expansion into an Asian market beyond the Chinese mainland and Hong Kong.
According to Baidu's latest earnings report and statement, Apollo Go delivered 3.4 million fully driverless autonomous ride-hailing trips in the fourth quarter of last year, representing over 200% growth year-on-year.

By February 2026, Apollo Go's global cumulative ride volume had surpassed 20 million trips.
In terms of operational mileage, Baidu's fleet has accumulated over 300 million kilometers of autonomous driving, with 190 million kilometers achieved in fully driverless mode.
The company disclosed its latest safety metrics in a statement, noting that airbags deploy only once per 12 million kilometers driven on average.
Alongside announcing the latest order figures, Baidu confirmed that Apollo Go has officially launched operations in South Korea, starting with the Seoul metropolitan area.
Elsewhere in Asia, Baidu has expanded its testing scope in Hong Kong and initiated cross-district testing. As the first right-hand drive market for Apollo Go, Hong Kong has previously been approved for designated passenger testing on open roads.
The expansion into the South Korean market is part of Baidu's recent acceleration of its global deployment. With operations now spanning 26 cities worldwide, Baidu is advancing its overseas rollout by forming alliances with global ride-hailing giants.
Earlier this month, Baidu and Uber announced a partnership to introduce Apollo Go to Uber's platform in Dubai next month. Users will be able to hail Baidu's sixth-generation autonomous taxis in designated areas like Jumeirah.
In Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, Apollo Go has also partnered with AutoGo to launch a fully driverless vehicle service.
In the European market, Apollo Go is advancing strategic collaborations with Uber and Lyft, planning to launch autonomous vehicle pilot programs in London, UK, during the first half of 2026.
The company has also initiated testing in the Swiss canton of St. Gallen in partnership with PostBus.

 Xpeng's robotaxis equipped with VLA 2.0 software have passed closed-venue testing and are set to begin public road tests.

{"url":"https://axis-intelligence.com/waymo-statistics/","title":"Waymo Statistics 2026: Rides, Revenue, Safety & Fleet Data - Axis Intelligence","text":"Axis Intelligence ResearchAxis Intelligence Research is our data journalism and market analysis division. Our research reports combine primary data analysis, industry surveys, and expert interviews to provide actionable intelligence for technology decision-makers. Each report undergoes peer review by at least two subject-matter editors before publication.

By Axis Intelligence Research

Co-author: Liam Michael | Last updated: July 5, 2026 | License: CC BY 4.0

Quick Answer

Waymo completed more than 20 million lifetime autonomous rides through December 2025 — tripling its annual volume in a single year — while logging 220.6 million rider-only miles by March 2026 across six U.S. cities. A $16 billion funding round in February 2026 valued the company at $126 billion, the largest capital raise in autonomous vehicle history.

According to Axis Intelligence Research’s analysis of Waymo’s official filings and CPUC-mandated reports: Waymo was delivering approximately 500,000 fully autonomous rides per week as of May 2026, up from 250,000 in April 2025. The fleet stood at roughly 3,700 Jaguar I-PACE vehicles, with a sixth-generation system now beginning deployment on the new Ojai platform. Annualized revenue reached $355 million as of February 2026.

Key Findings

Waymo completed 14 million fully autonomous trips in 2025 alone — more than triple the prior year — and surpassed 20 million lifetime rides by end of December 2025, according to Axis Intelligence Research’s analysis of Waymo’s official year-in-review disclosures.

The Waymo Driver logged 220.6 million rider-only miles through March 2026, achieving 90% fewer serious-injury-or-worse crashes than human drivers over the same distance in its operating cities, per Waymo’s NHTSA SGO-based Safety Impact Data Hub.

Waymo’s deadheading rate — the share of miles driven without a passenger — improved from 51.5% in January 2024 to 44.3% by September 2025, according to Axis Intelligence Research’s review of California CPUC quarterly filings; only 54% of total California miles were driven with a passenger aboard across the 14-month study period.

Waymo’s $126 billion post-money valuation in February 2026 implies a revenue multiple of approximately 355x on its $355 million annualized run rate, a ratio Axis Intelligence Research calculates by cross-referencing Alphabet’s SEC 8-K disclosures and Waymo’s publicly stated funding terms — a figure neither source states explicitly.

The average Waymo ride cost $19.69 in the San Francisco Bay Area during Q4 2025–Q1 2026, compared with $17.47 for Uber and $15.47 for Lyft — a 12.7% premium over Uber that collapsed from the 30–40% premium recorded just six months earlier, according to Obi’s 94,000-ride dataset.

Waymo Rides and Trip Volume Statistics

Waymo’s trip growth is the clearest measure of whether autonomous ride-hailing has moved from demonstration to operation. The answer, at this point, is unambiguous: it has.

From January to December 2025, Waymo’s year-in-review shows the company served more than 14 million autonomous trips — a figure that more than tripled its 2024 annual total. Riders spent over 3.8 million hours inside the vehicles. By December 2025, lifetime rides crossed 20 million.

The trajectory into 2026 continued the acceleration. Weekly paid rides hit 450,000 by December 2025, then crossed 500,000 by late Q1 2026, according to data referenced at the time of Alphabet’s Q1 2026 earnings.

{"url":"https://electrek.co/2026/10/22/tesla-cuts-2026-capex-guidance-q3-cash-flow/","title":"Tesla (TSLA) quietly cuts 2026 capex guidance to $20B","text":"Tesla has lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast. In its Q3 10-Q, the company now says it expects capital expenditures “to be in excess of $20 billion in 2026,” down from the “more than $25 billion” it had guided since April.

The change was in the 10-Q Tesla filed Wednesday, not in the shareholder letter it released the same day. And it lands in a quarter where Tesla reported $1.53 billion of positive free cash flow, a number that depends a lot on timing.

Tesla’s 2026 capex guidance keeps moving

Tesla started 2026 guiding to about $20 billion in capex. In April, it raised that to more than $25 billion, and in July, CFO Vaibhav Taneja reiterated the figure while Elon Musk called 2026 a “massive capex year.”

Now it’s back to “in excess of $20 billion.”

Tesla has spent $13.01 billion so far this year: $2.49 billion in Q1, $5.79 billion in Q2 and $4.73 billion in Q3. Hitting $25 billion would have required about $12 billion in Q4 alone, more than double its biggest quarter. The new floor only requires about $7 billion.

The 10-Q says 2026 spending is “driven by our SI initiatives, including investments in compute infrastructure and data centers,” along with factory ramps and Tesla’s fleet of “company-operated SI-enabled assets.”

There’s a catch in the cash numbers, though. Tesla had $3.67 billion of equipment and construction spending sitting in liabilities at the end of September, meaning it was booked but not yet paid. That’s up from $2.63 billion at the end of June and $1.63 billion a year ago. So Tesla’s actual spending is running ahead of the cash capex it reports.

Where Tesla’s Q3 free cash flow came from

Tesla reported $6.26 billion in operating cash flow and $1.53 billion in free cash flow after capex. Here’s how it got there:

Q3 2026AmountNet income$0.80BDepreciation, amortization and impairment+$1.85BStock-based compensation+$1.17BOther non-cash items (FX, taxes, bitcoin, SpaceX)-$0.15BChanges in working capital+$2.59BOperating cash flow$6.26BCapital expenditures-$4.73BFree cash flow$1.53B

Depreciation and stock compensation are normal add-backs. They reduce profit without using cash.

The working capital line is the one to watch. Without that $2.59 billion, Tesla’s free cash flow would have been about negative $1.06 billion.

Most of it came from bills Tesla hasn’t paid yet. Accounts payable rose $1.92 billion in the quarter and accrued liabilities rose $1.95 billion, including $722 million more in “accrued purchases,” goods Tesla received but hadn’t been invoiced for.

Another $1.26 billion came from deferred revenue, mostly energy storage. Tesla’s energy deferred revenue jumped to $3.30 billion from $2.31 billion. But not all of that is cash. Tesla disclosed that it billed SpaceX $588 million for Megapacks “that have not been delivered,” which SpaceX hadn’t paid at quarter-end. That amount sits in both deferred revenue and accounts receivable, which rose $565 million.

Those gains were partly offset by a $1.82 billion increase in prepaid expenses and other assets, and a small inventory build.

If you also count the $1.03 billion increase in unpaid capex, Tesla’s free cash flow on an “as spent” basis was closer to $500 million.

Tesla’s borrowing plans

The capex cut comes a month after Tesla signed $30 billion of new credit facilities. The 10-Q details them: a $20 billion delayed-draw term loan maturing in 2029, and $10 billion of revolving credit replacing a $5 billion facility. Tesla hadn’t drawn on either at quarter-end, and it had $45.4 billion in cash and investments.

Electrek’s Take

	None of this is improper in today’s accounting standards, which we can argue are pretty awful. Paying suppliers later, collecting deposits, and booking capex when it’s incurred are all somewhat normal accounting, and Tesla disclosed them. But they explain why the “$1.5 billion of free cash flow” headline from Wednesday’s results says less about the business than it seems.

Underneath, Tesla made $718 million of operating income, less than its $1.17 billion in stock compensation, and before working capital, it burned cash. The timing items that helped this quarter will reverse when the invoices come due and the Megapacks ship.

The capex cut is the more interesting signal. Six months ago, Tesla was telling investors 2026 would be a massive spending year to build out AI compute, Optimus and Cybercab. Now it’s lowering the target in its 10-Q instead of the shareholder letter, while lining up $30 billion of debt. Either projects are slipping into 2027, or Tesla is spending less to protect its cash. Tesla should say which.

{"url":"https://www.teslanewswire.com/articles/tesla-cuts-2026-capex-guidance-20-billion-from-25-billion-taneja-q3-earnings-call","title":"Tesla Cuts Its 2026 Spending Plan to $20B From $25B; Musk Says "Tens of Billions" in 2028","text":"The front page / Business / Stock & Deliveries
 BUSINESS / STOCK & DELIVERIES

 Tesla lowered its full-year 2026 capital spending guidance to $20 billion from $25 billion on its Q3 earnings call on Oct. 21, 2026, saying it would fund spending primarily from operating cash flow. Q3 capex was $4.732 billion and free cash flow was a positive $1.531 billion.
 By the Tesla News Wire staff · Edited by Seamus McKenna · October 21, 2026 · 2 min read
 Photo: Ministério Das Comunicações / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0 (cropped, resized). File photo from May 2022.
 Tesla now plans to spend $5 billion less this year than it said before. On its Q3 2026 earnings call on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, Tesla updated its full-year capital expenditure guidance to $20 billion, down from $25 billion, Yahoo Finance reported. Tesla's 10-Q, filed the same day, words it as capex "in excess of $20 billion in 2026," down from "more than $25 billion" (more from the 10-Q). CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the company is "managing our capital deployment efficiently" and plans to fund capex "primarily from our cash flows from operations."
The quarter's cash numbers (Tesla Q3 2026 update)

Capital expenditures: $4.732 billion (Q2 2026: $5.789 billion; Q3 2025: $2.248 billion)
Operating cash flow: $6.263 billion
Free cash flow: $1.531 billion, after negative $1.092 billion in Q2 2026
Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments: $45.447 billion, up $1.9 billion in the quarter

Yahoo Finance said analysts had estimated Q3 capex of $7.96 billion and free cash flow of negative $4.92 billion. CNBC noted free cash flow was still down 62% from a year earlier.
What Musk said about future spending
"I think capex is actually ending up being a little lower than we anticipated, but we'll start to become more meaningful next year. And then noticeable in the tens of billions in '28," Musk said on the call, according to Yahoo Finance. Yahoo said the money is going to Optimus production lines, AI compute, the Cybercab ramp and the Terafab chip plant Tesla is building with SpaceX.

Automotive Sales
Automotive sales revenue includes revenues related to cash and financing deliveries of new vehicles, and specific other features and services that meet the definition of a performance obligation under ASC 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (“ASC 606”), including internet connectivity, access to our FSD (Supervised) features and their ongoing maintenance, free Supercharging programs and over-the-air software updates. We recognize revenue on automotive sales, net of any discounts or financial subsidies, upon delivery to the customer, which is when the control of a vehicle transfers. Payments are typically received at the point control transfers or in accordance with payment terms customary to the business, except sales we finance for which payments are collected over the contractual loan term. We also recognize a sales return reserve based on historical experience plus consideration for expected future market values when we offer resale value guarantees or similar buyback terms. Other features and services such as access to our internet connectivity, unlimited free Supercharging and over-the-air software updates are provisioned upon transfer of control of a vehicle and recognized over time on a straight-line basis as we have a stand-ready obligation to deliver such services to the customer. Other limited free Supercharging incentives are recognized based on actual usage or expiration, whichever is earlier. We recognize revenue related to these other features and services over the performance period, which is generally the expected ownership life of the vehicle. Revenue related to FSD (Supervised) features is recognized when functionality is delivered to the customer and their ongoing maintenance is recognized over time. For our obligations related to automotive sales, we estimate standalone selling price by considering costs used to develop and deliver the service, third-party pricing of similar options and other information that may be available. Customers may purchase subscriptions, including FSD (Supervised) and premium connectivity, after taking delivery of their vehicles. Revenue from subscriptions is recognized either over time or point in time depending on the nature of contractual terms.
Any fees or financial subsidies that are paid or payable by us to a customer’s lender when we arrange the financing are recognized upfront as an offset against automotive sales revenue. As our contract costs related to automotive sales are typically fulfilled within one year, the costs to obtain a contract are expensed as incurred. Amounts billed to customers related to shipping and handling are classified as automotive sales revenue, and we have elected to recognize the cost for freight and shipping when control over vehicles, parts or accessories have transferred to the customer as an expense in cost of automotive sales revenue. Our policy is to exclude taxes collected from a customer from the transaction price of automotive contracts.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automotive sales, ex-credits | 78,509 | 72,480 | 65,821 | 55,573 | 81% → 71% | [S3][S4] |
| Automotive leasing | 2,120 | 1,827 | 1,712 | 1,098 | 2% → 1% | [S3][S4] |

| Total revenue | 96,773 | 97,690 | 94,827 | 78,669 | 100% | [S3][S4] |

Columns sum to the filed total; leasing reconciles 9M 2026 to $78,669m [S3][S4].

Regulatory credits fell 73% in Q3 to $113m, and Tesla reversed $475m of previously recognised credit revenue for contractual returns [S4]; the July 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act repealed consumer EV credits and restricted the programmes Tesla sells into [S3]. Tesla says it is cooperating with DOJ and SEC investigations and that no agency has concluded wrongdoing [S3]. Remedy cost is not disclosed.

**Governance.** Shareholders approved the 2025 CEO Performance Award on 6 November 2025 with 75% support, worth close to $1trn if market-cap and product milestones are met [S26]; the 10-K says the goals aim to focus Musk's time and that misalignment could waste capital [S3]. **Market size and growth.** Global EV sales are forecast at 22.7m units in 2026, only modestly above 2025 [S31]; the US fell 39.5% in Q3 2026 to a 6.4% BEV share after credits expired [S22]; grid storage is growing 41% [S28].

**Who is taking share.** BYD took the global BEV crown in 2025 with 2.26m units to Tesla's 1.64m and led Q2 2026 by 557,090 to 480,126, a 16% gap [S31]. Against Tesla's 1.32m deliveries in 9M 2026, BYD sold 3.13m vehicles including plug-in hybrids [S4][S29]. Xiaomi has stalled at 31,267 units in July 2026, 39% of a 550,000 target [S27]. **The most dangerous competitor is BYD.** On a like-for-like segment basis, BYD's automobiles and related products business earned a 22.33% gross margin in H1 2026 on RMB275.3bn of segment revenue, down 9.0% year on year [S48], compared with Tesla's 17.6% automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits in the same half (our arithmetic from filed 10-Q revenue and gross profit; 18.7% is reported for 9M 2026 including credits) [S4]. **Market size and growth.** Global EV sales are forecast at 22.7m units in 2026 [S31]; the US fell 39.5% in Q3 2026 to a 6.4% BEV share after credits expired [S22]; grid storage is growing 41% [S28].

| Market | Period | Figure | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Global EV sales, forecast | 2026 | 22.7m units | [S31] |
| US EV sales | Q3 2026 | 262,649 units, 6.4% share, −39.5% YoY | [S22] |
| Global storage deployments | 2026E | 158 GW / 459 GWh, +41% | [S28] |

**Who is taking share.** BYD took the global BEV crown in 2025 with 2.26m units to Tesla's 1.64m and led Q2 2026 by 557,090 to 480,126, a 16% gap [S31]. Against Tesla's 1.32m deliveries in 9M 2026, BYD sold 3.13m vehicles including plug-in hybrids [S4][S29]. Xiaomi has stalled at 31,267 units in July 2026, 39% of a 550,000 target [S27]. Baidu's Apollo Go peaked at 300,000 weekly trips in Q4 2025 and 20m cumulative across 26 cities [S47]; Waymo ran 500,000 paid rides a week by May 2026 with 3,700 vehicles and $355m annualised revenue [S45].

| Player | Latest volume | Price position | Share signal | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BYD | 557,090 BEVs in Q2 2026 | mass market, ASP $20,300* | 16% ahead of Tesla in Q2 BEVs | [S31][S32] |
| Tesla | 1.32m deliveries in 9M 2026 | ASP $41,300* | 54% of US EV sales in Q3 2026 | [S4][S32][S24] |
| Hyundai-Kia | 175,000 BEVs in H1 2026, +9.4% | mass market | 3.0% global BEV share | [S33] |
| Rivian | US EV sales +46% YoY in Q3 2026 | premium, ASP $90,700* | niche, gaining in a shrinking market | [S22][S32] |

*Third-party estimates (TrendX), same basis; low confidence. Geely sold 210,000 BEVs in H1 2026, +50%, a 3.6% share [S33].

**The most dangerous competitor is BYD.** On a like-for-like segment basis, BYD's automobiles and related products business earned a 22.33% gross margin in H1 2026 on RMB275.3bn of segment revenue, down 9.0% year on year [S48], compared with Tesla's 17.6% automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits in the same half (our arithmetic from filed 10-Q revenue and gross profit; 18.7% is reported for 9M 2026 including credits) [S4]. Company-wide they are level — BYD 18.85%, Tesla 18.7% — because BYD's electronics arm earned 5.04% [S48][S4]. We rely on the segment comparison: it strips that electronics drag and Tesla's credits, and shows BYD earning more per yuan of vehicle revenue at 49% of Tesla's ASP ($20,300 against $41,300, same estimate) [S32]. That removes Tesla's cost story. BYD's exports grew 154% and its Hungarian plant starts in late 2026, sidestepping the EU's 27% duty that protects Tesla [S29].

**Energy storage: a real second engine, not a counterweight.** Tesla deployed 36.0 GWh in 9M 2026 [S4], 7.8% of BNEF's 459 GWh 2026 forecast on a run-rate basis. Wood Mackenzie ranks Tesla the second-largest global BESS integrator behind Sungrow, with CATL third, BYD fourth and Fluence seventh [S46]. Segment gross margin rose from 18.9% in 2023 to 30.2% in 9M 2026 [S3][S4], arguing against pure commoditisation, but Megapack prices fell in 2025 [S3], Q3 revenue fell 16% [S4] and at 10.7% of 9M revenue it cannot offset cars [S4].

**Substitutes and moat.** Hybrids and plug-ins outsell BEVs, which were 6.4% of US new-vehicle sales in Q3 2026 [S22]. Charging is genuinely defensible: all major automakers have adopted Tesla's North American Charging Standard [S3]. Vertical integration is not: BYD is equally integrated at higher volume [S3][S4]. Software is an option, not a moat — $4.08bn of FSD-related deferred revenue against $78.7bn of 9M revenue [S4]. No cost per kWh is disclosed, so no cost advantage can be verified.

**Regulation and geography.** The US is smaller and credit-free [S3][S22]; Europe is where Tesla is losing fastest: January 2026 registrations fell 17% while the EU BEV market grew 14% [S30]; China is BYD's home market and Tesla's local volume is not disclosed [S3]. NHTSA's EA26002 covers 3.2m vehicles [S23].

**Counter-evidence: the case that Tesla loses the auto profit pool and has not monetised AI.** Revenue fell 2.9% in 2025 and was flat in Q3 2026 [S3][S4]; US volume fell 20% in a market down 39.5% [S22]; Europe has declined for thirteen consecutive months [S30]; BYD earns a higher automotive-segment margin at half the price [S48][S32]. Robotaxi has six metros against Waymo's fifteen and needs safety drivers in California [S25]. FSD has no revenue line: deferred revenue grew 5% in nine months [S4]. Against that, automotive gross margin recovered to 18.7% in 9M 2026 from 16.9% and Q3 total gross margin to 19.6% from 18.0% [S4] — the profit pool is shrinking in volume before it shrinks in margin.

Confidence: medium — volume and margin data are filed, but competitor totals come from trackers that disagree materially and Tesla discloses neither robotaxi nor FSD revenue.

Tesla closed at $404.22 on 28 October 2026, a $1,597.8B market capitalisation and a $1,561.6B enterprise value against $36.18B of net cash [S5][S4]. **Verdict: Sell, zero position, 12-month horizon.** Tesla is a flat car business at 15.1x EV/Sales against BYD's 0.89x, with 80–89% of the price — $322–359 a share — resting on robotaxi and AI revenue it does not report [S4][S39]. The probability-weighted band is $64/$142/$442 on 30/45/25%, or $194, 52% below spot; 9% bull upside does not pay for 65% base and 84% bear downside [S4][S5].

**Three positives.** Net cash of $36.18B, with trailing operating cash flow of $18,710M covering capex of $15,407M 1.21x [S4]. Q3 gross margin rose to 19.6% from 18.0% and automotive margin ex-credits to 17.5% [S4]. US EV share rose to 54% from 50.5% and storage gross margin reached 30.2% [S22][S24][S3][S4].
